preclude

prih-KLOOD -- the second syllable rhymes with 'rude'. · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To preclude is to prevent from happening; to make impossible.

The judge ruled that the signed waiver did not preclude the family from filing a lawsuit.

Example

A student breaks his wrist the week before tennis tryouts, and the doctor's order not to grip a racket for six weeks precludes any chance of competing.

The injury does not merely make tryouts harder; it makes them impossible. That is the force of preclude: to shut the door on something before it can happen at all.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

prevent: To prevent is the everyday word for stopping something from happening, by any means and to any degree -- you can prevent a cold or prevent a war. To preclude is stronger and more final: whatever precludes an outcome removes the very possibility, so the attempt never even begins.

avert: To avert is to ward off a specific danger just before it strikes -- you avert a crash, a crisis, a disaster -- and what is averted is always unwelcome. To preclude is quieter and broader: a condition makes an outcome impossible from the start, whether that outcome is good or bad.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

allow: to let something happen

enable: to make something possible

Where it sits · how completely and openly it blocks things — forestall → preclude → bar

forestall vs. preclude: Forestall is narrower and often gentler than preclude -- you forestall one particular problem by acting ahead of it, while something that precludes an outcome makes it impossible altogether.

bar vs. preclude: Bar can sound even more forceful than preclude: preclude often works quietly, as a condition that happens to make something impossible, while bar suggests an explicit block thrown up by a rule or an authority.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — pre-

Prefix — pre-: before (Latin prae-)

Root — clude

Root — clude: to shut, to close (from Latin claudere — the same root spelled clud/clus in include and exclusive)

Put it together

Put it together: Pre- ('before,' Latin prae-) + clude ('to shut, to close' — from Latin claudere): literally 'to shut beforehand.' Something that precludes an outcome closes the door on it in advance, before the possibility ever opens.

Use the root in a new word: include

Use the root in a new word: include: Remember to include your return address on the envelope.

Root Check

Word Choice

Preclude is the formal, stronger cousin of prevent: it means the possibility is gone entirely. It takes either a thing ('the rain precluded a picnic') or 'from' plus an action ('the rules preclude judges from voting'). If something is merely made harder, it has not been precluded.
